findings.title: Silent resolution of multiple CryptoProviders removes a useful safety check
findings.body: Previously detectProvider() threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath, which caught classpath/packaging misconfigurations early and loudly. Now it silently sorts by order() and picks the highest, logging the ignored providers only at debug level (which is typically filtered out in production). Worse, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order()==200, so if two of these full-featured providers accidentally end up on the same classpath (e.g. a packaging mistake bundling both the default and elytron crypto modules), the chosen provider now depends on ServiceLoader iteration order (effectively classpath/jar ordering), which is not guaranteed to be stable across environments. This can silently select the wrong crypto backend instead of failing fast, which is a real risk for a security-sensitive subsystem.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() does not actually return the BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The CryptoProvider interface documents getBouncyCastleProvider() as returning the BouncyCastle (or FIPS) security provider. This implementation instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. whatever provider happens to back the JVM's default keystore type (e.g. the SUN or PKCS12 provider), which has nothing to do with BouncyCastle. Any caller that relies on this method to obtain the actual BC provider (e.g. to reference its name or algorithms) will get a misleading/incorrect result when this is the active CryptoProvider.

findings.title: Dead code creates and discards ASN1Encoder instances
findings.body: In concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` construct encoders, write into them, and then discard the result without using it anywhere. This is leftover/dead code that wastes cycles and allocations on every signature conversion and should be removed.

findings.title: Single shared EC key reused for ES256/ES384/ES512 tests does not match expected curve sizes
findings.body: The test generates a single EC key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()` (no curve specified, defaulting typically to a 256-bit curve) and reuses it for testES256, testES384 and testES512. For ES384 and ES512, the real signature r/s values will actually be ~32 bytes (P-256 sized), not the 48/66 bytes implied by algorithm.getSignatureLength(). The round-trip only passes because integerToBytes() zero-pads/truncates to the expected length, masking the fact that the conversion logic is never exercised with genuinely 384-bit or 521-bit curve signatures. This reduces the test's value and could hide bugs that only manifest with real P-384/P-521 keys.

findings.title: New mandatory CryptoIntegration.init() call changes AuthzClient.create() behavior/contract
findings.body: AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now unconditionally calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), which throws IllegalStateException if no CryptoProvider implementation can be located via ServiceLoader on that classloader. Previously AuthzClient did not require any CryptoProvider to be present at all. Consumers that shade/repackage the authz-client jar in a way that drops or fails to merge META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider, or that load AuthzClient with a restrictive classloader, will now get a hard failure on client creation where they previously worked fine. This is a backward-incompatible behavior change that should be called out/tested explicitly.

findings.title: readInteger/readLength does not guard against indefinite-length (0x80) DER encoding producing negative array size
findings.body: readLength() returns -1 for the indefinite-length form (0x80) but this is not validated by callers. In readInteger(), `int length = readLength();` followed by `byte[] bytes = read(length);` will attempt `new byte[-1]` if length is -1, throwing an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException instead of a handled IOException. Since this decoder parses externally supplied DER-encoded signature bytes (attacker-influenced JWT/token signatures), malformed input can trigger an unexpected unchecked exception instead of a predictable IOException, which callers may not be prepared to catch.
